name: Syabrubesi
tagline: Road-head village where every Langtang trek begins and ends
meta_description: Syabrubesi (1,460 m) is the Langtang trek road-head, 122 km from Kathmandu. Drive times, lodges, hot springs and what to do before the trail.
summary: Syabrubesi is the road-head for the Langtang Valley, Tamang Heritage Trail and Yala Peak, a riverside Tamang bazaar at 1,460 m about 122 km and 7–8 hours by road from Kathmandu. Most trekkers spend one night here at the start and one at the end, sorting permits, porters and last supplies.
intro: Syabrubesi sits where the Langtang Khola meets the Bhote Koshi, a long street of lodges, tin-roofed shops and jeep stands squeezed between steep forested walls. It is the last place on the Langtang side with a reliable road connection to Kathmandu, which makes it the start and finish line for nearly every trek in the valley. Buses from Kathmandu roll in during the late afternoon, and by seven the next morning trekkers, guides and porters are crossing the suspension bridge towards Bamboo and Lama Hotel.

The village has two parts. Old Syabrubesi, on the upper terrace, keeps a few stone houses and a small gompa, while the newer lower bazaar along the river holds most of the lodges, money changers and gear shops. Many families are Tamang, and the Tamang Heritage Trail loops north and west from here through Gatlang, Tatopani, Thuman and Briddim before returning to the same street. North of town the road continues about 15 km to Rasuwagadhi on the Tibet border, the crossing used by Kailash overland groups heading for Kerung.

Syabrubesi suffered heavy damage in the 2015 earthquake and the road was cut for long periods afterwards; much of what you see today was rebuilt since. At 1,460 m it is warm for most of the year, so it is a comfortable place to rest a day after the drive or after coming down from Kyanjin Gompa. Expect basic but clean lodges, hot showers in most, and a lively evening scene in October and April when groups overlap.

highlights.title: Gateway to the Langtang Valley
highlights.text: The trail to Lama Hotel, Langtang village and Kyanjin Gompa starts at the suspension bridge at the east end of the bazaar. From here it is three walking days to Kyanjin at 3,870 m, climbing steadily through oak, rhododendron and bamboo forest along the Langtang Khola.

highlights.title: Start of the Tamang Heritage Trail
highlights.text: A separate loop heads west and north into Tamang villages that see far fewer trekkers than the main valley. Gatlang, Tatopani's hot springs, Nagthali ridge at 3,165 m and Briddim homestays sit within five walking days of Syabrubesi.

highlights.title: Old Syabrubesi and its gompa
highlights.text: A 20-minute walk up from the river bazaar brings you to the older village terrace, with stone houses, prayer flags and a small Buddhist gompa. It is a quiet way to stretch your legs after the long drive and to see how families lived before the road arrived.

highlights.title: The road to Rasuwagadhi
highlights.text: The road north follows the Bhote Koshi past Timure to Rasuwagadhi, Nepal's main road crossing into Tibet's Kyirong county. Kailash overland yatras via Kerung pass through Syabrubesi, and you will often see Tibet-bound trucks and pilgrim buses on the same road.

highlights.title: Rest stop after Kyanjin
highlights.text: Coming down from 3,870 m, Syabrubesi feels warm and green. A shower, a proper dal bhat and a cold drink by the river are part of the routine on the last night of most Langtang treks before the drive back to Kathmandu.

how_to_reach.text: Syabrubesi is about 122 km from Kathmandu via Kakani, Trishuli Bazaar, Betrawati and Dhunche. Local buses leave the Machhapokhari and Gongabu area early in the morning and take 7–8 hours; a private jeep takes 6–7 hours. The last 50 km above Betrawati is narrow, with landslide sections in the monsoon.

There is no scheduled air service, but charter helicopters can drop or collect groups near Syabrubesi in about 30 minutes from Kathmandu. This is mostly used for emergencies or by travellers short of time at the end of a trek.

Trekkers arrive on foot from Lama Hotel (about 5 hours down the Langtang Khola), from Briddim on the Tamang Heritage Trail (3–4 hours) or from Thulo Syabru on the Gosaikunda side (about 3 hours by trail or by the road).

where_to_stay: Lodges line the lower bazaar near the river and the bridge to the Langtang trail, with a smaller cluster on the upper terrace in Old Syabrubesi. Most are family-run teahouse lodges with twin rooms, attached or shared bathrooms, gas or solar hot showers and a dining hall serving dal bhat, noodles and pizza. Standards are simple and roughly similar; we choose rooms facing the river where possible, because the road side is noisier when early buses start their engines. There are no branded or star-rated hotels in Syabrubesi, so set expectations at clean and basic, and bring earplugs for the night before an early start.
tips: Take the earliest bus or jeep from Kathmandu so you reach Syabrubesi before dark on the mountain road.
Carry your Langtang National Park permit and passport where you can reach them; there are checkpoints at Dhunche and on the trail.
Withdraw cash in Kathmandu; ATMs in Syabrubesi are unreliable and lodges up the valley take cash only.
Buy snacks and toilet paper here, as prices rise with every hour you walk up the valley.
In the monsoon, check road conditions the evening before you travel, as landslides above Betrawati can close the road for hours.

experiences.title: Old Syabrubesi village and gompa walk
experiences.summary: A short climb from the river bazaar to the older upper village, with stone Tamang houses, prayer flags, a small gompa and views up the Bhote Koshi gorge towards the Tibet border. A good way to loosen up after seven hours on the road.
body: The lower bazaar of Syabrubesi grew up around the road, but the original village sits on a terrace above it. A stepped path climbs for about 20 minutes from near the bus stand, past maize fields and buffalo sheds, to a cluster of stone houses with carved wooden windows and slate or tin roofs. Prayer flags run between the rooftops and a small gompa sits at the top of the settlement.

From the upper terrace you look north up the Bhote Koshi towards Timure and Rasuwagadhi, and east to where the Langtang Khola cuts its gorge towards Lama Hotel. Your guide can explain how the village changed when the road arrived, and how families rebuilt after the 2015 earthquake damaged many homes here. Children often stop to practise their English, and older residents may be spinning wool or drying maize on the flat roofs.

The walk takes 1.5 hours at an easy pace and is suitable for anyone who can manage stairs. Go in the late afternoon when the light is warm and the day's buses have arrived. If the gompa is open, remove shoes, walk clockwise and leave a small donation. It is a useful first lesson in Tamang customs before you meet more of them on the trail.

faqs.q: Is the Old Syabrubesi walk difficult?
faqs.a: No. It is a 20-minute climb on stone steps and a farm path, then a level stroll around the upper village. Anyone who can climb two or three flights of stairs will manage. Allow about 1.5 hours in total including time at the gompa and viewpoints, and wear the shoes you will trek in so you test them on uneven ground.

faqs.q: Can we enter the gompa in Old Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Usually yes, if the caretaker is around. Remove your shoes, avoid pointing your feet at the altar and walk clockwise around any stupa or prayer wheels. Photography inside is sometimes not allowed, so ask first. A donation of NPR 100–200 in the box is a polite way to say thank you and helps with upkeep.

faqs.q: Do we need a guide for this walk?
faqs.a: You can find the path on your own, but a guide adds a lot. They can explain Tamang house design, the gompa's role in village life and how Syabrubesi changed after the road and the 2015 earthquake. On our treks the walk is led by your trek guide on arrival day at no extra cost.

experiences.title: Hot spring soak by the Bhote Koshi
experiences.summary: Soak tired legs in natural hot water pools near the Bhote Koshi after coming down from Kyanjin Gompa. A simple, local-style bath rather than a spa, best enjoyed in the cooler months on the last afternoon of a Langtang trek.
body: Hot water seeps out of the hillsides in several places along the Bhote Koshi valley, and near Syabrubesi it has been channelled into simple concrete pools used by villagers and trekkers. After a week of cold-water washes and long descents, half an hour in warm water is one of the most welcome moments of the whole trip. Ask your guide which pool is open, because the river and the monsoon regularly rearrange the banks.

Facilities are basic: a pool or two, a place to change and sometimes a small fee collected by the local committee. Bring a towel, sandals and a swimsuit; nudity is not acceptable and women usually bathe in a sarong or swimsuit with a T-shirt. Locals come in the evenings, so going in mid-afternoon gives you more space. Keep valuables at the lodge.

The best time is October to April, when the air is cool and the river is low. In the monsoon the river rises and pools can be flooded or closed. If you are trekking the Tamang Heritage Trail, the larger Tatopani hot springs at 2,607 m are on the route and make a fine comparison. Either way, a soak before the long drive back to Kathmandu helps stiff legs.

faqs.q: Are there hot springs near Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Yes, there are natural hot water outlets along the Bhote Koshi near Syabrubesi that have been made into simple pools. Their condition changes with floods, so ask at your lodge or let your guide check which one is open. On the Tamang Heritage Trail you also pass the better-known Tatopani hot springs at about 2,607 m.

faqs.q: What should I wear to the hot springs?
faqs.a: Wear a swimsuit, and women usually add a T-shirt or wrap a sarong, as many bathers are local families. Bring sandals for the wet concrete, a quick-dry towel and a bag for wet clothes. Leave your passport, phone and cash at the lodge. Nudity or skimpy swimwear will cause offence in this conservative rural area.

faqs.q: Can we use the hot springs in the monsoon?
faqs.a: Often not. From late June to early September the Bhote Koshi runs high and brown, and riverside pools may be flooded, silted or closed for safety. The best months are October to April. If you are in Syabrubesi during the monsoon, ask locally on the day rather than relying on what you read online.

experiences.title: Trek briefing and gear check with your guide
experiences.summary: The evening briefing in Syabrubesi covers the next day's route to Lama Hotel, altitude sickness signs, water, permits and porter loads. It is the best time to fix gear problems while shops and lodges can still help.
body: On the first night of a Langtang trek your guide sits down with the group after dinner to walk through the days ahead. Expect a clear outline of tomorrow's route: cross the bridge, follow the Langtang Khola through Domen and Bamboo at about 1,970 m, then climb through Rimche to Lama Hotel at about 2,470 m, roughly 6 hours on foot. You will hear where lunch is, where water can be refilled and which sections are steep.

The guide also covers altitude basics: walk slowly, drink 3–4 litres a day, and report headache, nausea or unusual tiredness early. Most Langtang itineraries reach Kyanjin Gompa at 3,870 m on day four and climb Kyanjin Ri at 4,773 m on day five, so understanding acclimatisation matters. Permits and passports are checked so nothing is missing at the Dhunche or trail checkpoints.

Then comes the practical part. Porters usually carry up to 15–20 kg shared between two trekkers, so bags are weighed and anything unnecessary is left at the lodge or in Kathmandu. Check boots, rain cover, headlamp, water purification and warm layers. Syabrubesi shops sell basic gloves, hats and ponchos if you forgot something, but choice is limited and quality varies.

faqs.q: How much can a porter carry on the Langtang trek?
faqs.a: Responsible agencies limit porter loads to about 20–25 kg including the porter's own kit, which usually means one porter for two trekkers with 10 kg each. We weigh bags at the Syabrubesi briefing. Pack light: two sets of trekking clothes, one warm layer set, a down jacket and toiletries are usually enough for 7–11 days.

faqs.q: Can I buy trekking gear in Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Only basics. Small shops sell gloves, woolly hats, ponchos, water bottles, snacks and sometimes cheap trekking poles. Proper boots, sleeping bags and down jackets are far better bought or rented in Thamel, Kathmandu, before you leave. Treat Syabrubesi as a last-chance stop for small items, not a place to equip a trek.

faqs.q: What is the first day of the Langtang trek like?
faqs.a: From Syabrubesi at 1,460 m you walk about 6 hours and 11 km to Lama Hotel at about 2,470 m, gaining about 1,000 m. The trail follows the Langtang Khola through subtropical and then oak and bamboo forest, with a few steep climbs after Bamboo. Langur monkeys are common and red pandas live in these forests, though sightings are rare.

faqs.q: How far is Syabrubesi from Kathmandu?
faqs.a: Syabrubesi is about 122 km north of Kathmandu by road via Trishuli Bazaar and Dhunche. Local buses take 7–8 hours and private jeeps 6–7 hours, depending on traffic leaving the city and road works above Betrawati. In the monsoon, landslides can add hours. Plan to arrive by late afternoon and start walking the next morning.

faqs.q: What is the altitude of Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Syabrubesi lies at about 1,460 m on the Bhote Koshi, roughly the same height as Kathmandu. That means no altitude issues on arrival. The trek then gains about 1,000 m on day one to Lama Hotel and reaches Kyanjin Gompa at 3,870 m by day three or four of walking.

faqs.q: Is there a bus from Kathmandu to Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Yes. Local and semi-tourist buses leave from the Machhapokhari and Gongabu area of Kathmandu early each morning, usually between 6:30 and 8 am. Tickets are cheap, but seats are tight and the bus stops often. Shared and private jeeps are faster and more comfortable. Check current departure times and fares before you travel, as they change.

There may be one or two ATMs or bank branches, but they are often out of service or limited by card type. Carry enough Nepali rupees from Kathmandu for the whole trek, roughly NPR 3,500–5,000 per day if you are paying your own meals, plus tips. Lodges above Syabrubesi accept cash only.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit to stay in Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Syabrubesi itself is outside the core trekking area, but you will pass the Langtang National Park checkpoint at Dhunche on the drive and need your park entry permit to start the trek. Foreign trekkers also need a TIMS card and, under the rules in force since 2023, a licensed guide. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How many nights should I spend in Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: One night at the start and one at the end is standard. A second night at the start is wise only if you arrive very late or feel unwell after the drive. On the Tamang Heritage Trail you will also pass through or near Syabrubesi on the final day, so many itineraries simply drive back to Kathmandu from there.

Yes. It is a working road-head village with lodges used to families and trekking groups. The main hazards are traffic on the single street and the fast Bhote Koshi river, so keep children away from the banks. Lodges are simple but have private rooms, and the warm climate at 1,460 m suits children well.

faqs.q: Can I go from Syabrubesi to Tibet?
faqs.a: The road continues about 15 km north to Rasuwagadhi, Nepal's border crossing to Kyirong in Tibet. Only travellers with a Chinese visa and Tibet permits arranged through an authorised agency can cross, typically on Kailash overland yatras via Kerung. You cannot simply walk across from a Langtang trek. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there mobile signal in Syabrubesi?
faqs.a: Yes, Nepal Telecom and Ncell both have 4G coverage in Syabrubesi most of the time, and many lodges have Wi-Fi. Signal becomes patchy beyond Bamboo and Lama Hotel, then returns in parts of Langtang village and Kyanjin Gompa. Buy a local SIM in Kathmandu with your passport before leaving.
